chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Faddal from Hafs and others of our companions from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
He was asked about a man who swears to his brother [to eat with him]; he said: There is no penalty upon him, for he only intended to honor him.
Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from al-Wassash from Aban ibn Uthman from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who swears to another man to eat food, but he does not eat; is there a penalty upon him for that? And what is the oath upon which a penalty is obligatory? He said: The penalty is for the one who swears regarding an item that he will not sell it or buy it, then it occurs to him [to do the opposite], so he expiates his oath. And if he swears regarding something, and doing it is better than leaving it, let him do what is better, and there is no penalty upon him. That is merely from the steps of Satan.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Wasshash from Abd Allah ibn Sinan from a man from Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) who said: When a man swears to his brother regarding what he fulfills his oath upon, then upon the swearer is the penalty of the oath. The way to reconcile this narration is to carry it upon a type of preferability (istihbab) rather than obligation (fard/wujub).
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on an oath to eat with someone if they do not eat, and when is an oath expiation (kaffarah) obligatory?
ai.summary: This passage from *Al-Istibsar* clarifies the fiqh of oaths (*yamin*) by distinguishing between casual social gestures, such as inviting a companion to eat, which carry no expiation if unfulfilled, and binding commercial vows. It further elucidates the principle that breaking an oath to perform a superior act (*khayr*) requires no penalty, while specific oaths regarding property transactions do, reflecting the Shia scholarly emphasis on intent (*niyyah*) and context in legal rulings.
